frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong bargaining power as a major gas supplier, but European efforts to diversify imports limit long-term leverage. Hydrocarbon revenue remains exposed to price volatility and external demand.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Russian defense ties, Chinese infrastructure involvement, and European energy engagement give Algiers strategic options, while also creating pressure to avoid overdependence on any single partner.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic logistics
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting major United States, European, and Gulf interest because of its route toward critical minerals in the Copperbelt. Angola gains infrastructure and bargaining power, but must prevent the corridor from becoming an enclave serving foreign supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to fiscal stability and exports, leaving national resource security vulnerable to declining production, price shocks, and foreign-operated upstream assets.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel insecurity spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity along the northern frontier threatens transport corridors, agricultural zones, and planned energy and mining investment. Benin is strengthening regional and international security cooperation while trying to preserve sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Regional trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Cotonou remains deeply tied to Nigerian and wider West African commerce, creating exposure to border restrictions, informal trade networks, and changing regional political alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial leverage through its partnership-based diamond sector, but dependence on global diamond demand and established foreign marketing networks constrains flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: External investors are seeking access to Botswana's copper, nickel, and other mineral prospects. The government must balance investment and infrastructure needs against risks of concession-driven extraction with limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization pressure
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production, refining, and marketing while challenging foreign mining arrangements. This may increase fiscal sovereignty but risks investment disruption, smuggling, and reduced technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced dependence on former Western partners but creates new external leverage and does not resolve the territorial threat to mining zones and transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Informal Mineral Trade
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other minerals continue to move through opaque regional networks, limiting state capture of value and increasing exposure to foreign traders and sanctions risk.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain tense, while insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo complicates border control, trade routes, and sovereignty over mineral flows.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Backed Port Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port and logistics development draws interest from European, Chinese, and other external partners, creating opportunities while raising concerns over long-term strategic access and debt exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Imported Energy and Water
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel, food, and desalination inputs leaves the islands vulnerable to shipping disruptions and external price shocks despite expanding renewable capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Access Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign financiers remain important to roads, rail, ports, and extractive projects, giving external partners leverage over strategic corridors and future resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far-North Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the northwest and southwest, alongside insurgent threats in the Far North, disrupts agricultural, energy, and transport networks and weakens effective state control.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-Minerals Arrangements
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and political partners retain major influence around mining and regime protection, constraining transparent licensing and national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Weak Transport Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and insecure borders leave commercial access dependent on foreign-backed security and neighboring transit routes, enabling armed groups and external actors to capture resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's oil exports depend heavily on the Cameroon pipeline corridor and foreign operators, limiting autonomous control over transport, pricing, and revenue realization.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan War and External Security Ties
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in Sudan strains border management and humanitarian capacity while increasing the strategic value of Chad's territory to foreign security and regional power networks.

frictionVectors.title: French control and Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains effective control of Mayotte, sustaining a core sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' control over surrounding maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: External aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and energy development remain heavily dependent on foreign donors and investors, constraining autonomous economic planning.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-backed investors continue to dominate processing, finance, and export channels for strategic minerals, limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Regional proxy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east involves armed groups, regional interests, and competing diplomatic alignments, weakening Kinshasa's effective control over territory and mining corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues and offshore production remain central to the economy, leaving the state vulnerable to external operators, price volatility, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and resource projects strengthen connectivity but can narrow fiscal and contractual autonomy when revenues underperform.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cocoa value chains
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has improved regulation and producer support, but multinational traders and processors still capture substantial value beyond the farm gate.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's expansion strengthens national leverage, while reliance on foreign capital, imported equipment, and external security partnerships remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: The presence of multiple foreign military facilities provides revenue and deterrence but also limits strategic autonomy and makes Djibouti vulnerable to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: China-linked infrastructure and competition with neighboring ports create debt, revenue, and sovereignty risks around critical trade corridors.

highlights: Gulf and IMF capital deepen dependency

frictionVectors.title: External financing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large IMF-backed adjustment needs and Gulf investment provide liquidity but increase outside influence over strategic assets, land, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, keeping Egypt exposed to upstream water-management decisions and regional power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms, trading houses, and external lenders remain central to monetizing declining offshore reserves, limiting autonomous resource planning.

frictionVectors.title: Gas monetization bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: LNG and gas-processing infrastructure offer leverage, but aging assets and limited domestic capacity constrain diversification beyond hydrocarbons.

highlights: Red Sea position raises strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract competing regional and external security interests, increasing pressure on its sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: State-linked mining arrangements provide revenue and foreign exchange, but opaque contracts and limited transparency weaken domestic accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African transport, electricity, customs, and investment networks, reducing room for independent infrastructure and trade policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and textile exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export industries depend on preferential market access and foreign buyers, leaving employment and state revenue vulnerable to changes in trade regimes.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD has increased Ethiopia's bargaining power over regional energy and water, but tensions with Egypt and Sudan remain a major sovereignty risk.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on external finance limit policy flexibility while foreign-backed transport, telecom, and energy projects expand strategic influence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign influence over extractives
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state control over oil, manganese, and mining concessions while balancing longstanding French ties with Chinese and other investor interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependency
frictionVectors.details: Gabon’s export economy depends heavily on externally financed and operated rail and port infrastructure, limiting room for autonomous resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on Senegal
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia’s security, trade, and transport options remain closely tied to Senegal, creating practical constraints on independent regional policy.

frictionVectors.title: Banjul port modernization
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to improve port and transport infrastructure could strengthen sovereignty, but financing and commercial dependence on external partners remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: External financing constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on international financial support narrow policy space, especially for infrastructure and energy investment.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and gold leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining damages land and water resources while weakening formal state control of gold, with foreign financiers and domestic networks both implicated.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects, particularly Simandou, rely on foreign capital, railways, and port infrastructure, creating long-term bargaining risks despite potential state revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Junta-centered resource governance
frictionVectors.details: The military-led transition is using mining agreements and infrastructure commitments to build legitimacy, but weak transparency increases exposure to external leverage and elite capture.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export concentration
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on raw cashew exports leaves producers vulnerable to foreign buyers, price shocks, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Political instability and trafficking
frictionVectors.details: Institutional fragility and suspected transnational trafficking networks weaken state control over ports and borders, increasing reliance on regional and international security partners.

highlights: Strategic balancing between China, Gulf investors, and Western lenders
Infrastructure diplomacy shifts toward tighter sovereign bargaining

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and external debt servicing constrain Nairobi's policy space. Chinese-financed transport infrastructure and Gulf-backed port interests remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is competing with regional ports and corridors while seeking foreign capital for Lamu and Mombasa. Security risks in northern Kenya and the Red Sea raise the strategic cost of these projects.

highlights: Water exports remain the kingdom's core strategic asset
Economic dependence on South Africa limits autonomy

frictionVectors.title: South African water dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue but structurally ties national infrastructure and water policy to South African demand and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and labor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The garment sector depends heavily on external trade preferences and foreign-owned manufacturers. Any disruption in United States market access or regional supply chains would quickly affect employment and fiscal stability.

highlights: Mining revival attracts competing foreign capital
Port and concession governance test national control

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore and gold projects are central to growth but leave Liberia exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and uneven local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port modernization and transport corridors require substantial external financing. Concession terms and access to regional trade routes remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided by rival institutions
Foreign security patrons shape the political balance

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities and armed groups can disrupt production, export terminals, and budget flows. Foreign-linked commercial and political networks continue to influence access to Libya's energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: External military entrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, and regional actors retain influence through security partnerships, contractors, and political ties. This limits unified sovereign control over strategic bases, borders, and energy infrastructure.

highlights: Resource governance struggles to outrun political volatility

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining operations are dominated by foreign capital and export markets, creating jobs and revenue but limiting domestic processing and bargaining power over strategic minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Mining infrastructure and local consent
frictionVectors.details: Ports, roads, and power systems linked to mining projects can operate as foreign-controlled enclaves. Land disputes, environmental damage, and weak consultation periodically generate resistance around major sites.

frictionVectors.title: IMF austerity and creditor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Malawi's debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms constrain fiscal autonomy while external creditors shape spending, exchange-rate, and subsidy policy. Import dependence leaves the country vulnerable to foreign-exchange and fuel-supply shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals without reliable power
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in uranium, rare earths, and graphite is increasing, but weak electricity and transport infrastructure limit local value capture. The government faces pressure to offer investor incentives without repeating opaque or low-return concession practices.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The military government relies heavily on Russian-linked security support as it distances itself from France and regional institutions. This relationship may improve regime protection but increases opaque payments, political dependency, and civilian-risk exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Gold control and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains the state's crucial foreign-exchange asset, yet informal mining, foreign operators, and armed-group taxation complicate national control. Conflict around mining zones and transport corridors continues to threaten production and public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas project dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers Mauritania new revenue and diplomatic leverage, but offshore infrastructure and foreign operators retain substantial control over technology, finance, and marketing. Border coordination and revenue expectations remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Mining logistics and external capital
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore expansion and rail upgrades depend on international finance, specialized contractors, and port access. Nouakchott is seeking more domestic processing and fiscal returns while managing dependence on foreign mining partners and Chinese-linked infrastructure demand.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty transition
frictionVectors.details: The future administration of the Chagos Archipelago and the Diego Garcia security arrangement remains a major sovereignty and great-power issue. Mauritius must balance territorial claims and compensation with the strategic interests of the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: Blue-economy infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius relies on external partners for port modernization, subsea connectivity, maritime surveillance, and energy security. Competition among India, China, Western states, and Gulf investors creates leverage but requires careful non-alignment.

highlights: Phosphate and green power consolidate leverage

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource politics
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and development of Western Sahara underpins its Atlantic strategy but remains contested by the Polisario Front and Algeria. Investment, fisheries, renewables, and export infrastructure in the territory continue to generate legal and diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is leveraging ports, rail, renewable energy, and the Nigeria-Morocco gas corridor to strengthen regional influence. These projects depend on foreign capital and technology, exposing Rabat to competition among European, Gulf, Chinese, and U.S. partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Resumed gas development depends heavily on multinational capital and external security support. Delays and local grievances limit Maputo's leverage over the project and its revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten gas infrastructure, transport corridors, and state authority. The government's reliance on foreign and regional forces exposes a persistent sovereignty gap.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: New oil, uranium, lithium, and green-hydrogen projects are attracting major outside investors. Namibia is seeking stronger local-content and fiscal terms, but financing and technical dependence remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Capacity
frictionVectors.details: Ports, electricity, water, and rail capacity may constrain the conversion of mineral and energy discoveries into domestic value. Foreign-backed infrastructure will expand capacity while increasing negotiation pressure on the government.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Recontrol
frictionVectors.details: The military government is pressing foreign mining interests for greater state participation and strategic control. Political confrontation and legal uncertainty could reduce investment and constrain production.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Breaks with Western partners and regional institutions have disrupted trade, aid, and security cooperation. Dependence on alternative external partners may replace one form of influence without restoring infrastructure resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Failure
frictionVectors.details: The state continues to lose production and revenue through theft, sabotage, and aging infrastructure. Foreign operators retain substantial technical and financial influence while communities contest environmental and fiscal outcomes.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Gas Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity could reduce fuel-import dependence and improve bargaining power. Gas-processing, pipeline, and power-sector bottlenecks still leave Nigeria exposed to external capital and unreliable infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral-trading position is increasingly scrutinized over alleged links to supply chains originating in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Diplomatic pressure and traceability demands threaten access to premium markets.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state control over strategic policy but depends on external partnerships, aid, and security relationships. Regional tensions can convert that diplomatic capital into sanctions, trade restrictions, or infrastructure risk.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons attract foreign operators, but limited discoveries and weak state capacity constrain bargaining power. São Tomé and Príncipe remains exposed to unfavorable terms if exploration accelerates.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, telecoms, and energy upgrades depend heavily on external finance and contractors, creating modest sovereignty risks despite the country's small strategic footprint.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-operated oil and gas
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers major fiscal leverage but leaves Senegal dependent on international partners, export infrastructure, and volatile global prices. Contract renegotiation and local-content demands could strain investor relations.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects rely on foreign lenders and contractors, while fiscal pressures limit Dakar's room to retain a larger share of resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of maritime assets
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles seeks outside investment in ports, fisheries, tourism, and maritime surveillance while balancing Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf interests. Infrastructure partnerships can improve capacity but narrow strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing agreements and distant-water fleets generate revenue but raise concerns over monitoring, local value capture, and depletion of marine stocks.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining companies and export logistics dominate the minerals economy, leaving Sierra Leone vulnerable to commodity cycles and disputes over taxation, environmental damage, and local benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external financiers support roads, energy, and construction, but repayment obligations and project-selection politics can limit sovereign control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign port and security deals
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, and other external actors compete for access to ports, military facilities, and maritime corridors. These partnerships provide security and revenue but risk fragmenting federal authority and long-term control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource and fisheries pressure
frictionVectors.details: Oil exploration and foreign fishing interests are expanding amid limited enforcement capacity. Weak regulation, piracy risks, and federal-regional disputes make it difficult for Somalia to convert maritime resources into broadly shared sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: RAIL AND PORT CAPACITY
frictionVectors.details: Chronic constraints at Transnet railways and ports limit the state’s ability to capture full value from minerals and agricultural exports. Private operators and foreign investors are gaining influence as infrastructure financing gaps persist.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY TRANSITION CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking investment and partnerships for electricity reform, renewables, and battery minerals while trying to preserve domestic processing and industrial policy leverage. External capital remains important but can dilute sovereign control over strategic supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE ON SUDAN
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan’s oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving production, revenue, and maintenance exposed to armed-group disruption and external bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN OIL AND SECURITY INTERESTS
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies and neighboring states retain major leverage over production, transport, and payments. Weak institutions and limited diversification reduce Juba’s ability to convert resource wealth into sovereign development.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD NETWORKS AND EXTERNAL SPONSORS
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trade remain central to financing competing armed actors, with regional commercial and political networks influencing routes, refining, and access to hard currency.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND PIPELINE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Sudan’s Red Sea port, oil-export infrastructure, and internal transport corridors. Foreign powers can gain leverage by providing arms, logistics, or infrastructure support to rival authorities.

frictionVectors.title: LNG DEVELOPMENT TERMS
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large offshore gas projects involve major international energy companies and require Tanzania to balance fiscal returns, local-content demands, environmental concerns, and investor certainty.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port, and logistics projects are expanding Tanzania’s regional influence while creating long-term exposure to external lenders, operators, and competing Indian Ocean interests.

frictionVectors.title: PORT-DEPENDENT SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo’s role as a regional trade hub, but dependence on foreign shipping, logistics, and finance limits the state’s control over strategic infrastructure and transit revenues.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE AND INDUSTRIAL FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Togo is attempting to increase domestic value capture from phosphate resources while relying on external capital, technology, and markets. Debt and governance constraints remain obstacles to deeper sovereign beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: European migration and budget pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European cooperation, financing, and market access while resisting demands linked to migration control. This creates sovereignty concerns without amounting to direct resource capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and electricity vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic energy output and reliance on imported gas and electricity constrain policy autonomy. External investment in renewables is strategically useful but may deepen dependence if local value capture remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and environmental exposure
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline ties Uganda's petroleum strategy to foreign capital, operators, and export infrastructure. Land acquisition, environmental risks, and financing restrictions continue to generate sovereignty and implementation friction.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, hydropower, and industrial projects expand connectivity but increase exposure to foreign contractors, debt obligations, and imported inputs. Uganda retains formal control while bargaining power remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining contest
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt investment from Chinese, Gulf, and Western-linked firms is expanding, giving Zambia leverage but also exposing it to competition over concessions and processing terms. The central challenge is retaining more refining, tax, and technology value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Transport corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper exports depend on rail and port corridors through neighboring states, leaving Zambia vulnerable to transit bottlenecks and foreign infrastructure decisions. Corridor diversification is improving resilience but remains incomplete.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance of mineral projects
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain prominent in lithium, platinum, gold, and diamond operations. Export controls and beneficiation rhetoric have increased state leverage, but weak institutions and opaque licensing limit effective domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power and currency constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, foreign-exchange instability, and sanctions-related financial isolation raise operating costs and push mining firms toward external financing and self-supplied infrastructure. This strengthens investors' negotiating position against the state.
